title: IMF warns bond yields could see a 'disorderly' spike as debt, inflation risks worsen
content: BANGKOK – The International Monetary Fund warned Tuesday that government bond yields could rise in a disorderly fashion, as rising inflation, mounting debt and AI-related borrowings pressure sovereign bond markets. Government bond yields in several advanced economies have climbed to multidecade highs, driven by higher energy costs due to the Middle East conflict and expectations for tighter monetary conditions as central banks look to curb resurgent inflation. In its latest Global Financial Stability Report, the fund warned that sovereign bond risk could deteriorate, warning of "a sharp rise in sovereign bond yields." The report was released Tuesday as part of the IMF-World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok, Thailand, this week, where more than 18,000 delegates gathered to discuss the state of the world economy and the financial system. High debt load and rollover risks make the bond market "susceptible to more frequent fiscal and inflation shocks," the report said. The IMF had warned last week that global public debt had reached near its highest level since World War II and was on track to soon exceed 100% of GDP. "Impact could be severe given the foundational importance of sovereign bond markets," the IMF said Tuesday. A sharp rise in yields would mark down asset values through higher discount rates, including for AI-related assets, and erode the value of government bonds posted as collateral. IMF also noted the exponentially rising borrowing by AI firms — that compete with sovereign bonds for investor demand — as an additional source of strain on bond markets. Hyperscalers' share of global investment-grade bond issuance has risen to 10% from less than 1% since 2024, the report said. The global AI buildout has seen tech giants, such as Alphabet Inc's Google, Meta Platforms , hyperscalers and AI labs raising hundreds of billions of dollars in debt this year. "AI-linked issuance – much of it longer-dated – has grown large enough to compete with government bonds for investor capital, even if it does not appear to be the dominant driver of yields," according to Marc Seidner, CIO of non-traditional strategies at Pacific Investment Management. Hedge funds' growing holdings of Treasuries leave the market "susceptible to a disorderly unwind," the IMF said. Leveraged basis trades have partly unwound without notable pressure in the short-term loan market but the leverage that remains is a concern. Hedge funds' share of U.S. Treasuries rose to about 9% in 2025 from about 4% in 2022, mostly through highly arbitraged strategies, the IMF said, citing data from the Federal Reserve. Caio Ferreira, IMF deputy division chief for financial supervision and regulation, said the worry stems from hedge funds' rising leverage and their increasingly overlapping positions, meaning multiple funds are holding the same trades, potentially amplifying impact from a collective unwinding. On the bright side, liquidity has held up in the U.S., Europe and the U.K., the IMF said. Japan is the exception: liquidity in its government bond market has "continued to deteriorate" as yield volatility has risen since the end of yield curve control. The fund urged debt managers to lengthen maturities, warning that rollover risk could be exacerbated by strategies that replace long-term debt with short-term borrowing on a large scale. The IMF sounded the alarm over a web of "circular" financing deals among AI firms. Since 2023, 14 publicly disclosed deals channeled about $300 billion of equity, led by hyperscalers, into financially weaker AI firms, alongside $650 billion of debt. In exchange, the investors secured $1.4 trillion of "future revenue commitments" through services or chip orders, the IMF said. The revenue promises are what set the deals apart, Jason Wu, assistant director of the IMF monetary and capital markets department, said at a press briefing on Tuesday. "What makes this a little bit unusual compared to previous deals is the future revenue commitments, hence the circularity." If AI commercialization falls short, the losses could arrive together. "If there are questions about the monetization in AI, the equity investments will deplete in value, the debt may be difficult to service, and the revenue commitments in the future may not materialize," Wu said, describing what he called a "triple whammy." Such heavy financing and revenue promises cluster in a handful of AI firms, the report said. Due to that concentration, "there are certain companies and nodes that are particularly exposed," Wu said. "If there are some kind of issues with those entities, then the circularity would pose risk to the market."

title: SK Hynix, SoftBank shares plunge as tech stocks in Asia track Wall Street chip sell-off
content: Asian technology stocks fell Tuesday as a sell-off in U.S. semiconductor shares spilled into regional markets, with worries over artificial intelligence financing and intensifying competition denting sentiment. Shares of South Korean chip giant SK Hynix, a leading supplier of high-bandwidth memory chips used in artificial intelligence applications, plunged more than 8%, while rival Samsung Electronics shed 7.9% — both hit their lowest intra-day levels since August. In Japan, shares of tech-focused investment giant SoftBank Group sank 8.03%. The group, which has significant exposure to the global AI industry, led a broader retreat in Japanese semiconductor and electronics shares. Tokyo Electron , a major supplier of chipmaking equipment, dropped 6.6%, while Advantest , which makes semiconductor testing equipment, declined 5.38%. Other Japanese technology stocks also came under pressure. Lasertec fell 4.76%, Disco lost 4.83% and Renesas Electronics shed 5.89%. The declines followed a weak session for technology stocks on Wall Street, where the Nasdaq Composite dropped 0.44% on Monday. U.S. memory chipmaker Micron Technology slid 3.9% as investors assessed intensifying competition from China's ChangXin Memory Technologies, or CXMT , which reported progress on a new chip structure. Over the weekend , CXMT announced significant progress in developing a new chip architecture, designed to increase memory density by packing more data into a smaller space. "Investors are jittery and looking for excuses to take profit on AI-related stocks that have outperformed this year, especially memory stocks," said UBP's senior equity advisor Vey-Sern Ling. "In reality, while the Chinese memory makers can potentially become a threat to global demand-supply balance over time, in the short run they continue to face technology hurdles, especially for more advanced memory like HBM," Ling told CNBC via email. CXMT shares were down over 2%. Phillip Wool, chief market strategist at Rayliant Global Advisors, said CXMT's breakthrough marked a significant milestone for Chinese chipmakers , demonstrating their ability to overcome technology restrictions and potentially challenge established players sooner than expected. But he cautioned that the market reaction appeared disproportionate to the immediate competitive threat, given that CXMT has yet to demonstrate large-scale production and continues to lag Samsung and SK Hynix in market share. "More importantly, we're not even talking about HBM here, and the Korean chipmakers are still unquestionably dominating that space, with very little threat at all from the likes of CXMT or anyone else for the foreseeable future," Wool said. He said the sharp sell-off reflected broader anxiety over the AI trade rather than a fundamental shift in the competitive landscape. "I read that more as a sign of how vulnerable AI sentiment is at this moment," Wool said, warning that volatility could persist as investors reassess chip demand and how long semiconductor manufacturers can sustain their pricing power. The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom have warned that access to capital could emerge as a major headwind to the AI boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply. Investors are also looking ahead to a busy week of corporate earnings and U.S. inflation data, which could provide fresh clues on the outlook for interest rates that often have an inverse correlation with growth stocks.

Monday - Friday, 6:00 - 7:00 PM ET The stock market has given investors plenty of reasons to sell over the past four years. CNBC's Jim Cramer said those who resisted the temptation have reaped the rewards. Since bottoming on Oct. 12, 2022, the S&P 500 has surged roughly 118%, weathering aggressive Federal Reserve rate hikes , a banking crisis , sweeping tariffs and a war in Iran. The rally began amid widespread pessimism about inflation and the economy, yet none of those setbacks managed to derail it . "The real lesson is that there never seems to be a good time to invest, because bad things do happen quite regularly, and yet investing is a superior way to get a return," the " Mad Money " host said. The gains have been substantial. According to Cramer, a $10,000 investment in the S&P 500 at the October 2022 bottom would now be worth nearly $23,061. Some of the market's biggest winners delivered even greater returns. Nvidia surged roughly 1,875% over that period, turning a $10,000 investment into approximately $197,505. A $10,000 investment in Meta Platforms would have grown to more than $58,800 as shares climbed 488%. Cramer's Charitable Trust , the portfolio run by CNBC's Investing Club, owns shares of Nvidia and Meta. For Cramer, the bigger takeaway isn't about picking the next market leader. It's about staying invested through uncertainty rather than trying to time every downturn and recovery. "We could not have predicted either the big declines or the big rebounds," Cramer said. "We could've turned tail so many times in these four years. And we would've been all the poorer for it." Cramer talked further about why he always stays in the market in his Sunday column for Investing Club members . Club analyst Zev Fima wrote a follow-up story Monday, using an investment calculator that you can plug your own numbers into to show the power of compound interest. The cost of missing a market rally can be substantial. According to JPMorgan , an investor who put $10,000 into the S&P 500 and missed its 10 best trading days between 2005 and 2024 would have ended up with less than half the wealth of someone who stayed fully invested. "Stay in, keep buying, don't lose faith," Cramer said. "Those are the lessons from this indomitable four-year-old bull market." title: Elon Musk gives $276 million to Republican groups, becomes biggest known 2026 midterm donor
content: Elon Musk spent more than $276 million in newly disclosed donations to Republican groups since July, making him the biggest known donor of the 2026 midterm election as the party fights to hold its majorities in Washington this November. The largest share – $158 million – went to the Senate Leadership Fund, the main super PAC backing Republican Senate candidates, according to figures provided by Musk's representatives to The New York Times and confirmed Monday to CNBC by Lindsey Curnutte, a spokesperson for Musk's America PAC. The Tesla and SpaceX CEO also gave more than $76 million to America PAC , the group he founded during the 2024 election, which has built a large voter-turnout operation in competitive Senate and House races . The new contributions bring Musk's known federal political giving for the 2025-26 cycle to roughly $366 million, already surpassing the approximately $290 million he spent during the 2024 presidential election . The scale of the latest giving is historic: Musk's $158 million contribution to Senate Leadership Fund is among the largest known political donations by an individual in U.S. history. The new figures were disclosed days ahead of a Thursday Federal Election Commission filing deadline , when political committees are due to report their third-quarter finances. The Senate Leadership Fund has spent heavily this cycle to defend the Republican majority, including in Texas, where GOP Attorney General Ken Paxton is running against Democrat James Talarico . Talarico leads Paxton 48.4% to 45.0% in FiftyPlusOne's polling average as of Oct. 12. Musk separately gave $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC , which supports Paxton. He also contributed $20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund , the leading super PAC supporting House Republicans, $10 million to the Republican Governors Association and $2 million to the Republican Attorneys General Association, the Times reported and Curnutte confirmed. The trillionaire's footprint in Texas has expanded rapidly in recent years, with Tesla, X and The Boring Company now headquartered in the state and SpaceX growing its manufacturing and launch operations there. The political spending is also a sharp reversal from Musk's public comments last year. "In terms of political spending, I'm going to do a lot less in the future," Musk said in May 2025. At the time, Musk was stepping back after a highly visible role in President Donald Trump's administration and a public falling-out with the president. The two have since repaired their relationship, appearing together at several recent events. Musk also retains deep ties to the federal government through SpaceX, a major NASA and Pentagon contractor . Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth last month also named him co-director of Project Meridian , a Pentagon panel studying the future of warfare. — Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

title: IonQ to acquire cybersecurity firm Elisity in an all-stock deal for up to $1.3 billion
content: Quantum computing platform IonQ said on Monday it will acquire cybersecurity company Elisity in an all-stock deal worth up to $1.3 billion, including up to $150 million in performance-based earnouts. The move is designed to defend against and uncover attackers targeting generative artificial intelligence large-language models and AI agents, and to protect against emerging quantum threats, the companies said in a press release . CEO Niccolo de Masi told CNBC's Morgan Brennan on Monday that the addition of Elisity's platform will help bolster his company's quantum security strategy. "This means that we can protect not only critical infrastructure — we believe better than anyone in the world — but of course the Fortune 500," de Masi said. The all-stock deal is expected to close in the fourth quarter, subject to regulatory approval, and would expand the quantum-computing company's cybersecurity portfolio. IonQ shares fell more than 9% in afternoon trading. Other quantum computing stocks, including Rigetti Computing and D-Wave Quantum , also traded lower. Elisity will retain its current leadership, including CEO James Winebrenner. IonQ's stock has surged in recent months amid a buying spree. Most recently, the company bought semiconductor maker SkyWater Technology for $1.8 billion in July. In the past year and a half, IonQ has acquired several quantum companies, most notably U.K.-based quantum computing startup Oxford Ionics . The deal follows two June executive orders from President Donald Trump aimed at building a quantum computer for scientific research by 2028 and protecting government systems from cyber threats. IonQ said in the release that the orders underscored the urgency of preparing for quantum computing threats. De Masi told CNBC on Monday that the need for quantum-level security integration into government and business as outlined in the executive order will become all-important as "Q-Day" — the era where quantum computers can break today's standard encryption software — draws closer. "Lab leaks" from frontier AI companies such as OpenAI 's high-profile Hugging Face hack are just the beginning compared to cyber capabilities a year from now, de Masi said. "Our technologies help you today. They also set you up, of course, as well as you can today, for an era where the bad guys will eventually get quantum computers. They will eventually be able to marry them, I fear, with LLMs, and so the world that we're in today is already dangerous," De Masi told CNBC, adding that LLM's "could do even more dastardly things." "Frankly, people are not ready," he said.

title: Meta debuts Muse Wonder AI model in latest test of users' willingness to pay
content: Meta debuted its latest artificial intelligence model, Muse Wonder, and says it's the most advanced option for powering digital assistants. But it doesn't come for free. To access the model, users of the Muse personal agent app will need to sign up for a monthly subscription of $20 or $100. The release underscores Meta's efforts to create new AI-derived revenue sources outside of its core online ad business . Meta AI chief Alexandr Wang said in an interview on Monday that the company developed Muse Wonder, codenamed Watermelon, to improve the capabilities of "personal and professional agents" so they don't stumble on tasks like booking dinner reservations and checking for availabilities. "When you do real-world tasks, you're going to get roadblocks and you're going to get things that come up or various setbacks," Wang said. "We specifically tried to train the model to be able to try other approaches instead of stalling and then checking back in with the user at any time." Meta said in a blog post that the latest model "offers our strongest safeguards to date" against "cyber misuse." Those protections only come with the paid model for now. Muse shot up to the top of Apple's App Store after Meta introduced the AI agent app last month. The app is free, with subscription plans available for more usage. Wang said Meta's AI team has been monitoring for agent-related "incidents or issues" with Muse in order to understand problems and resolve them. Some users have complained on social media that the agent accessed personal messages without authorization, which the company has disputed . Meta is trying to better inform people of how to use the app to avoid certain problems, Wang said. "I think there are certainly instances users have authorized various communications or whatnot earlier in a conversation, and then may have forgotten about that," Wang said. He added that the company is educating users on such matters "to ensure that consumers can trust the product going forward." Muse Wonder will also be available to coders who pay to access the company's related Meta Model API . Wang said that offering will cost more than the standard subscriptions because it is a "much larger model and at frontier level." He said it will still be priced "meaningfully below" leading models from OpenAI and Anthropic. An even more powerful variant of Meta's latest model, dubbed Muse Wonder Full, will only be available to developers who sign up to the company's software engineering focused Muse Code AI agent under a $50 or $200 a month subscription plan. title: Microsoft to rely more on homegrown AI chips, reducing dependence on Nvidia
content: Microsoft will ramp up use of its homegrown artificial intelligence chips after years of reliance on Nvidia's graphics processing units, as the software giant attempts to bolster its AI stack. Starting with its third-generation Maia AI accelerator, unveiled on Monday, Microsoft said it will mainly rely on its own silicon to handle incoming requests. Microsoft's greatest strength in AI has been its Azure cloud, which runs a series of models for clients. Its Microsoft 365 Copilot and GitHub Copilot offer AI-powered services to software engineers and other office workers. And the company develops in-house models, though they've yet to make a big splash in a market dominated by OpenAI , Anthropic and Google . The emerging opportunity in chips stems from unrelenting demand for advanced processors and a desire in the market for choice. Nvidia's GPUs have been the standard for AI workloads and models, and they fill Microsoft's existing data centers, while also serving to train models from OpenAI and Anthropic. But as demand keeps growing, the model leaders have embraced a variety of silicon from companies including Amazon , Advanced Micro Devices , Cerebras , Google and, in recent months, Microsoft. For general-purpose use, Microsoft already taps its own central processing units as well as silicon from Intel and AMD . Finance chief Amy Hood said at a Goldman Sachs conference last month that use of its own chips has helped with "margin improvement over the course of a decade." Microsoft introduced its inaugural AI chip, the Maia 100, in 2023 . It touted the Maia 200 this past January , and CEO Satya Nadella told analysts in July that Maia 200 "delivers 30% better performance per dollar than the latest generation hardware in our fleet" and said it was handling OpenAI models. Production of the Maia 300 starts in 2027. Microsoft is targeting multi-gigawatt deployments of chips in the Maia family, according to a blog post from Executive Vice President Scott Guthrie. But Alistair Speirs, a general manager, declined to provide a timeline. "We reserve a little bit of optionality there, because this is an industry that's changing very fast, and we want to deploy the right silicon for the right models that we're using at the right time as well," Speirs said. Microsoft expects to pack 96 Maia 300 chips into each data center rack, double the number for the Maia 200. The new version can run through up to seven times more AI tokens per rack, with 40% more tokens per megawatt when compared with GPUs. "We need new architectures that will give us essentially better performance, better use of the power that we have," Speirs said. "You can think of power translating pretty directly into operational cost for something like a data center as well." Parts of Microsoft 365 Copilot should speed up with Maia 300, said Jim Kleewein, a technical fellow at the company. In a note distributed to clients on Wednesday, Evercore ISI analysts estimated that Maia will represent about 10% of Microsoft's spending on AI chips by the first quarter of 2027. The analysts recommend buying Microsoft shares. Nvidia will still be a big part of the equation. CEO Jensen Huang spoke at an event last week where Microsoft announced a Surface laptop containing an Nvidia processor. And when it comes to training models, Microsoft partners with Nvidia and AMD, Speirs said. Unlike Google's tensor processing units or Amazon's Inferentia and Trainium, Microsoft's accelerators can't be rented by the hour to other companies. "Nobody has tested them outside of Microsoft yet," said Patrick Moorhead, CEO of advisory firm Moor Insights and Strategy. WATCH: Melissa Otto: Nvidia is the bellwether of the AI trade

title: 5 Things to Know
content: This is CNBC's Morning Squawk newsletter. Subscribe here to receive future editions in your inbox. Happy Monday. I saw "The Social Reckoning" over the weekend, the first of a string of new movies and TV shows focused on technology executives. Stock futures are little changed this morning. Stocks finished last week higher. Here are five key things investors need to know to start the trading day: Following a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, President Donald Trump on Friday said that Moscow would supply more than 4 million tons of diesel to the global market. The deal comes as Trump faces pressure to bring Americans relief at the pump before the midterm elections, but analysts are skeptical the agreement will lead to lower prices. Here's what to know: Independent evaluators once occupied a quiet corner of the artificial intelligence world. Now, as safety concerns mount, they're being tapped to help get the industry on the right track. AI titans are turning to third-party evaluators such as Model Evaluation and Threat Research (METR) and Transluce to monitor their models. As CNBC's Ashley Capoot reports, the role of these organizations has become even greater in the absence of a federal government safety framework. Speaking of AI safety: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella became the latest industry leader to voice concern over AI risks, writing on social media Saturday that the technology needs an "emergency brake." Nadella said models should be built with containment and independent controls. The Justice Department is investigating whether the White House television press pool violated antitrust laws by suspending their coverage of Trump when the president banned CNN, MS NOW and Politico from accessing the White House. The DOJ said it is looking at whether the press pool's pause in coverage broke the Sherman Act, a federal law prohibiting agreements that unreasonably restrain trade. Members of the press pool — which includes CNN, Fox News, ABC, CBS and NBC — did not immediately respond to CNBC's requests for comment. Meanwhile, Katie Zacharia, a lawyer and conservative commentator, will take over as White House press secretary today. Zacharia succeeds Karoline Leavitt, who left the Trump administration in August and is expected to begin a role at Fox News next month. French bond yields are trading near levels last seen in 2002. Some investors are wondering whether Italy could face a similar fate as the country considers widening its budget deficit. The Italian government is set to present a budget that includes recently confirmed allocations for defense and energy. The new spending levels could enlarge Italy's deficit over the next two years and make its debt-to-GDP ratio the highest in Europe, according to Goldman Sachs. As a result, Italy's government bonds could feel more pressure heading into the country's general election next year. Still, some investors see Italy as better off than France thanks to its largely domestic bond ownership. Retailers are trying to clean up their balance sheets. To do so, many are taking products off of their shelves. As CNBC's Ryan Baker writes, less inventory can help businesses stabilize sales and reduce the likelihood of ending up with a glut of product. But on the other hand, fewer items leaves shoppers with fewer choices. That's a compromise many well-known retailers have made amid surging energy and food prices. Brands from Dollar General to BJ's Wholesale Club to Lululemon have all announced plans to reduce the number of products they sell. title: Intel, Broadcom CEOs warn capital crunch could become AI's biggest bottleneck
content: SINGAPORE — The chief executives of Intel and Broadcom warned that access to capital could emerge as a major constraint on the artificial intelligence boom, even as demand for computing infrastructure continues to outstrip supply. Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said financing could become a bigger obstacle to AI expansion than shortages of semiconductors, memory chips or electricity, as the industry races to build the infrastructure needed to power increasingly sophisticated models. "[What] I think might be the biggest constraint is capital," Hock Tan said at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore on Monday. Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan echoed concerns about financing, pointing to the rising cost of capital and questions over whether companies investing heavily in AI will eventually generate sufficient returns. "If there's any challenge in the front, it's capital and the cost of capital, and then the other part is in the longer run, people want to see the ROI," he said. Their remarks highlight an emerging challenge for the AI industry, which has poured enormous sums into data centers, advanced chips and power infrastructure in anticipation of surging demand for computing capacity. The warnings come as rising borrowing costs threaten to complicate financing for technology companies investing heavily in AI infrastructure. Higher bond yields could make it more expensive to fund data center construction and chip purchases, potentially putting pressure on the economics of projects that may take years to generate returns. Hock Tan said the industry has repeatedly encountered supply bottlenecks over the past two years, but expects some of those constraints to ease as production capacity expands. "[In the] last two years we have seen a series of bottlenecks that keep coming out, but then we overcome it," he said. "Memory shortage today might not be that way a year from now." He suggested that wafer shortages could ease by 2028 or 2029, while power availability could also improve as new infrastructure comes online. Despite the financing concerns, both executives remained bullish on near-term demand for AI computing infrastructure. "There is more demand for compute infrastructure than we can supply," Hock Tan said, adding that the imbalance could persist through 2029 and potentially into 2030. Intel’s Tan similarly said the industry was unlikely to experience a significant slowdown over the next two to three years, citing growing adoption of AI applications and demand for computing power. But sustaining that growth beyond the next few years will depend on how quickly businesses adopt AI and whether the technology delivers meaningful economic benefits, the executives said. Broadcom’s Tan cautioned that demand for computing infrastructure could slow if the adoption of advanced AI models disappoints or improvements in their capabilities begin to plateau. Lip-Bu Tan, meanwhile, emphasized that companies would increasingly need to demonstrate tangible returns from AI investments through improved efficiency and new business models.

title: World Bank jobs council urges 'crisis-era' employment support measures as IMF warns of AI ‘tsunami’
content: BANGKOK — Policymakers are moving from debating whether artificial intelligence will hit jobs to issuing stark warnings about AI-led disruption and recommending measures on cushioning the fallout. International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Monday that artificial intelligence was hitting the global labor market like a "slow-moving tsunami," with young graduates first in line to be knocked down. "People to worry about, first and foremost, [are] young people that are coming into the labor market," Georgieva said at a panels on Monday. "Normally, they would get into these routine, repetitive jobs and then grow up the ranks. But if they're gone, I don't think any young person wants to be a barista in a coffee shop as ... professional future." Speaking on the same panel, Singapore President Tharman Shanmugaratnam, who co-chairs the World Bank's Jobs Council, called for governments to make "crisis-era" support measures a permanent tool for getting young people into work. What governments did during the Covid-19 pandemic and, in some cases, the global financial crisis "now has to be thought of not as a crisis measure, but as part of the structural, the menu of structural policies," he said. That means working with the private sector, and incentivizing firms to hire fresh graduates, because "the first rung in employment, your first job upon graduation, is now seeing less demand," Shanmugaratnam said. The remarks show that policymakers are moving from debating whether AI will disrupt jobs to deciding how to cushion the fallout, at a time when rapidly aging populations, particularly in Asia, already threaten to shrink workforces. World Bank President Ajay Banga, estimates 1.2 billion young people will turn 18 over the next 15 years, and the private sector, which already generates 75% to 85% of jobs in any country, will have to absorb most of them. The IMF estimates that about 40% of jobs worldwide will eventually be "augmented, downgraded or eliminated." Exposure is about 60% in advanced economies and 23% in low-income countries, she said, but poorer nations are not better off: that is "just because AI is further away." The squeeze is clearest in tech, Shanmugaratnam said, adding that in the U.S. "for the first time in a century, demand for graduates has gone down," with the wage premium for a college degree also shrinking. Without action, a cohort of graduates loses more than a year of skills: "you lose trust in the future," he said. Banga, however, is less pessimistic about the disruption to the job market from AI. "Large language models are estimated probably to create some degree of disruption in jobs in the developed world," he said. "But by the time you get to middle-income countries and lower-middle-income countries, actually, the opportunity from small AI to build jobs and build productivity is enormous," he told CNBC on Tuesday. AI has also been the major driver propping up growth this year. AI-related investments and trade have lifted output in a handful of economies, helping keep global expansion near 3% despite an energy supply shock, Georgieva said. "Love it, hate it, or fear it. It [AI] is here, and we are already seeing the first wave of impact," Georgieva said, estimating AI adoption could lift growth by 0.5 percentage point to 1 percentage point in advanced Asia, and 0.2 percentage point to 0.8 percentage point in emerging Asia. At the high end, that "would more than offset the loss that comes from aging population," said Georgieva. Shanmugaratnam cautioned that growth alone may not necessarily deliver job creation. China, India and developing Southeast Asia are "growing quite well, but job creation is weak," he said, and AI "is going to widen that divergence if we are too passive about it." AI-induced job displacement, however, will come "task by task," he said, "and that gives us time" — provided workers can learn on the job and universities shift toward applied training.

By the time animals left their first unmistakable fossils, they may already have had up to 200 million years of evolutionary history behind them. A fossil deposit in Mongolia preserves microscopic organisms in extraordinary detail, down to cells inside specimens that resemble embryos. Yet none of the fossils examined can confidently be identified as an animal, even though fossils from Namibia and South China show that animals already existed when the Mongolian deposit formed. That gap challenges an assumption researchers have used to date the origins of animal life. If a deposit preserves tiny organisms exceptionally well, can scientists conclude that any animals alive at the time would also have been preserved? A new study led by the University of Oxford, published in Science Advances on October 2, suggests the answer is no. Revisiting that assumption pushes the possible origin of animals up to 200 million years before their first unmistakable fossils. Animal fossils seem to appear relatively suddenly just before the Cambrian Period, which lasted from 539 to 487 million years ago, despite other evidence pointing to an earlier evolutionary history. Researchers have recently used the roughly 590-million-year-old Weng’an Biota in China to limit how far back that history could extend. Its rocks, dating to the Ediacaran, preserve microscopic organisms in exceptional detail, but none are definitive animals. Scientists therefore inferred that animals must have originated after the deposit formed, reasoning that it would have preserved them had they existed. The Mongolian deposit, known as the Kheseen Biota, offers a way to examine that reasoning. It is more than 40 million years younger than Weng’an, although the two share some species, and dates to a time when animals are known from elsewhere. The research team, which included scientists from the University of California, Berkeley, ETH Zürich, and Yale University, conducted a comprehensive survey of its exceptionally preserved microfossils. They examined more than 140 samples, including material from previously undocumented localities, using scanning electron microscopy. Alongside the embryo-like fossils with internal cells, they identified new microfossil species, including acritarchs, tiny spherical organisms with spines and branching projections. Senior author Associate Professor Ross Anderson, of the University of Oxford’s Museum of Natural History, said, “The Kheseen Biota breaks the argument that the exceptional microfossils of Weng’an mean we would have seen animal fossils in the assemblage had they existed at the time. The Kheseen microfossils are just as well-preserved, yet animals continue to be absent—despite the fact we know at that point they existed.” The earliest animals would have been small and soft-bodied, lacking the shells, bones, and other hard structures that make later animals easier to preserve. Fossilization would have depended on their environment and an unusual combination of chemical conditions after death. The researchers argue that animals either lived in environments different from those represented in the Kheseen Biota or that the chemical conditions there failed to preserve their remains. Either possibility weakens the use of Weng’an’s missing animals as evidence that animal life had not yet begun. Chemical traces offer another way to look for creatures whose bodies have disappeared. Biomarkers preserved in ancient rocks provide evidence consistent with sponges living at least 650 million years ago, tens of millions of years before the oldest definitive macroscopic animal fossils, those large enough to see without a microscope. To estimate how much further back animal origins might reach, the team used molecular clock analysis. This technique compares genetic differences between living species and combines rates of evolution with fossil dates as reference points to estimate when their ancestors lived. The dates supplied by the fossil record help constrain those estimates, so changing them can alter the inferred evolutionary timeline. Instead of treating Weng’an as the maximum age for animal origins, the researchers drew on several older deposits dating from roughly 850 to 730 million years ago. These included the Svanbergfjellet Formation in Norway, the Bitter Springs Group in Australia, and the Chuar Group in Arizona, United States. All are rich in fossils and have the potential to preserve animals, although animal fossils have eluded discovery in them. These deposits have previously been used to set maximum dates for animal origins. Using those older geological constraints shifted the estimated origin of animals back by around 200 million years compared with analyses constrained by the younger Ediacaran Weng’an deposit. The resulting estimate, between 800 and 700 million years ago, places their possible beginnings deep in the Neoproterozoic Era. That interval spans the beginning of the Cryogenian Period, around 720 million years ago. During the Cryogenian, enormous glaciers spread across the planet in episodes commonly known as Snowball Earth. Animals could therefore have evolved before some of Earth’s most extreme ice ages or appeared during that inhospitable interval. The findings reopen questions about whether conditions associated with Snowball Earth helped shape the origin and early evolution of animal life. First author Orin Lole Durbin, now a PhD student at Virginia Tech and an undergraduate at the University of Oxford at the time of the study, said, “Pre-Ediacaran animal body fossils still elude us, and this analysis does not prove that animals existed 800 million years ago. However, our new fossil evidence from Mongolia undermines one of the main arguments for restricting animal origins to the Ediacaran interval. Meanwhile, our molecular-clock analyses show how much further back their evolutionary history could extend.” The researchers recommend searching deposits from different parts of the world that represent varied environments and ways of preserving fossils. That search should consider all available evidence, including animal bodies, traces of their activity, and chemical biomarkers. Anderson added, “Until that evidence becomes available, the precise birth date of the animal kingdom remains uncertain.” Reference: “Re-evaluating molecular clock maximum age calibrations revives pre-Ediacaran divergence estimates for animals” by Orin M. Lole Durbin, Eliel S.C. Anttila, Derek E.G. Briggs, Francis A. Macdonald and Ross P. Anderson, 2 October 2026, Science Advances . For decades, a doomsday equation predicted population growth better than most experts, until falling birth rates undermined its forecast of catastrophe in 2026. In 1960, Science , one of the world’s leading science journals, published an article with an unambiguous title: Doomsday: Friday, 13 November, A.D. 2026 . It predicted that on this future date—just over a month from today—the human population would approach infinity and effectively annihilate itself. The outlandishness of the claim landed the article in widespread public attention. More surprisingly—because its underlying research and math seemed sound—it also received careful and sustained scientific attention. The authors—Heinz von Foerster, an Austrian-American professor and cybernetics expert, and two of his students, Patricia M. Mora and Lawrence W. Amiot—argued that human populations are exceptional and might grow beyond an exponential rate, at an ever-increasing one. “Our great-great-grandchildren will not starve,” they argued. “They will be squeezed to death.” The article was regularly cited, and its predictions appeared remarkably accurate—until around 1993, halfway to the predicted “doomsday,” when the global population began falling behind its forecasts. Today, the global birth rate is slightly less than half what it was in 1960 . Hopefully, we will all wake up on Nov. 13 to an ordinary day. Nonetheless, this article remains exemplary for blending rigorous science with the art of stagecraft to a staggering effect. The mid-20th century saw increasing societal concern about global population growth and its potential to lead to resource scarcity and geopolitical conflict. Underlying much of this concern was implicit or explicit acceptance of the Malthusian idea that whereas population has the potential to grow exponentially, it is kept constantly under check by its capacity to feed itself . In their article, however, von Foerster and his co-authors argued that as far as populations go, humans may be exceptional. Given our capacity to communicate and form “coalitions” that help us resolve problems, rising population density might simply mean more opportunities for collaboration, so that our numbers might grow not only beyond an exponential rate but at an ever-increasing one. They then used 24 estimates of the world population stretching across the past 2,000 years to show that human numbers have in fact continually outpaced expectations. All this was presented in calm, scientific prose and aided by dense mathematical equations. Von Foerster and his co-authors then projected these historical figures into the future, calculating that thanks to ever-increasing growth, in the year 2026 our numbers would near infinity. Thankfully, the same capacity for collaboration that assisted our species’ development throughout history could now avert this catastrophe. Since we are unlikely to want to reduce our life spans, they concluded, we should work together to reduce the global birth rate by half. This publication caused an immediate stir. There were stories in Time and The New York Times . It became the subject of a series of Pogo comic strips, and many commentators took the article as strictly a tongue-in-cheek comment on population fears. Rather than the story dying out, a funny thing happened. When Science published letters to the editor from mathematicians and demographers attacking von Foerster and his colleagues’ work—calling it “ridiculous” and “manifestly absurd”—the authors responded with spirited defenses that doubled down on the underlying math and its conclusions. Throughout the 1960s through to the 1980s, the “doomsday” equation became regularly cited—usually at face value—in textbooks on genetics, ecology, and demography. It appeared in stranger places, too. In a 1963 Canadian parliamentary committee , for example, a witness from the chemical industry prominently cited it as the reason chemical pesticides were required: to feed the approaching population explosion. In a 1971 U.S. Supreme Court abortion case leading up to Roe v. Wade, it was cited as why there was no compelling reason for the government to favor increased population. The doomsday idea persisted in part because its predictions for future populations turned out to be highly accurate—at least for a while. Its core equation yielded projections that were better than those of most demographers throughout the 1970s and 1980s . Only around 1993 did that accuracy begin to falter, and the global population began falling behind the forecasts—because the world began to do what von Foerster and his colleagues recommended it do. Today, the global birth rate is slightly less than half the 1960 rate. We will probably not all wake up on Friday, Nov. 13, “squeezed to death.” But before simply moving on—prepping for the next doomsday scenario—it is worth asking what we can learn from this one. For me, the lesson is in how we present our beliefs to the world. Heinz von Foerster was, at one point in his life, a stage magician. Borrowing the classic language of stagecraft, an effective illusion relies on three parts: the setup, the extraordinary turn, and the final reveal that returns the situation to normal. Von Foerster and his co-authors’ article gained attention because it was an ordinary scientific article wrapped in an extraordinary title and conclusion. It retained significance because it was firmly grounded in research and argument. To draw the world’s attention to a serious matter by way of absurdity—that’s a good trick. title: NASA may already have proof life once existed on another planet. Scientists might never get to find out
content: A leopard-spotted rock that could prove whether life ever existed beyond Earth is sitting in a tube on Mars. NASA’s Perseverance rover grabbed up the sample, called Sapphire Canyon, from rocky outcrops on the edges of the Neretva Vallis, a valley sculpted by rivers that once flowed into an ancient lake in Jezero Crater more than 3 billion years ago. The rover landed at the dried lakebed in February 2021 for expressly this purpose, hunting for rocks created or modified by water in the past, which would have had the best chance of preserving evidence of life. Members of the Perseverance science team have said the Sapphire Canyon sample, about the size of a chalk stick, is exactly the type of rock they hoped the rover would discover. “This is the first time I think we’ve found something that qualifies as a ‘potential biosignature’” on Mars, said Adrian Broz, a member of Perseverance’s science team and a postdoctoral researcher in the Planetary Surface Processes Lab at Purdue University in Indiana. “It’s currently sealed inside of Perseverance rover’s chassis, and it sits there quietly and awaits return to Earth.” But the sample might not make it to our planet, at least not anytime soon. The Mars Sample Return program, a joint venture by NASA and the European Space Agency to ferry the promising cache back to Earth, attracted intense scrutiny for its high price tag and complex design. After sinking billions of dollars into the endeavor, NASA paused and began reassessing the program in 2024 before canceling it entirely — with no clear alternative in sight. “While Perseverance’s samples remain safely stored on Mars, NASA is exploring a range of potential return options that could offer simpler and more affordable approaches than the original Mars Sample Return plan, including possible commercial or international contributions,” the agency said in a statement shared with CNN in July. NASA’s leaders still haven’t revealed a path forward. And while the discovery of the Sapphire Canyon sample is building a strong case for the existence of ancient microbial life on Mars, there’s only so much scientists can learn from afar, said Dr. Briony Horgan, professor of Earth, atmospheric and planetary sciences at Purdue University. The rover, which cost NASA about $2.4 billion to build and launch, doesn’t have the instrument suite to answer such lofty questions by itself on the red planet. “We can keep doing these studies and coming up with these hints, but we’re never going to know for sure until we get those samples back,” said Horgan, also a coinvestigator and planner on the Perseverance team. “These samples are our best current chance for really understanding is life abundant and common, or is Earth truly unique?” Now, it’s possible one of NASA’s biggest competitors in the new space race will be the first to achieve Mars sample retrieval: China is looking to pick up its own souvenir from the red planet in 2031, and it has taken steps to ensure success by designing a mission that’s similar to one it pulled off two years ago. But the rocks returned by the country’s Tianwen-3 mission, expected to launch in 2028, could look very different — and perhaps offer different insights — from Perseverance’s samples, depending on how plans evolve. Scientists consider Sapphire Canyon such a promising find because of its spotted appearance. On Earth, the tiny dots, called reaction fronts or reduction spots, form in soils and sediments due to the presence of microbial activity. “When there’s organic matter that’s lodged in sediment or soil that’s buried and microbes start to digest some of that organic matter, they form these bleached halos and spots that are quite resemblant to the ones that Perseverance found in this ancient river valley,” said Broz, coauthor of a study about the rock sample published in September 2025. Perseverance drilled the Sapphire Canyon sample from an arrowhead-shaped rock called Cheyava Falls in July 2024. The mudstones surrounding the rock were also covered in hundreds of thousands of promising reduction spots potentially made by ancient microscopic life. Still, returning the samples to Earth is the only way to determine whether these distinctive features were formed by the presence of life, or abiotically — through chemical or geological processes that did not require life, Broz said. It’s a lesson planetary scientists learned from studying the famed Allan Hills 84001 Martian meteorite , uncovered in the Antarctic in 1984 and originally thought to contain the remnants of ancient life. Multiple groups of scientists analyzed samples from the meteorite, discovering that nonbiological, geological processes left behind signatures that could be misinterpreted as organic carbon compounds attributed to life. “Even when you have all the labs all over the world looking at a rock that has putative evidence of ancient life, it is a really difficult thing to do, and so you want to just be able to apply every technique you can think of in all the best labs,” said Ashwin Vasavada, project scientist for the Curiosity rover at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, California. The rover’s onboard tools can offer some data, but they weren’t designed to do the kind of analysis necessary to make definitive answers because that wasn’t part of the original plan. “The science instruments had been selected with the assumption that they would be doing reconnaissance for sample selection and providing the geologic context on Mars for samples that were always expected to be returned to Earth,” said Dr. Melissa Rice, a professor of planetary science at Western Washington University who has worked on NASA rover missions for over two decades. The first entry in NASA’s budget request to Congress for initial studies of a Mars sample return program occurred in the fiscal year 1978, according to Casey Dreier, chief of space policy at The Planetary Society. The request was made on the heels of the agency’s Viking missions to Mars, considered NASA’s first attempt to search for evidence of life on the red planet. “It tells you how long it has remained this kind of scientific holy grail for Mars,” Dreier said. A 2003 survey identifying top scientific objectives for future space missions — and several subsequent reports — highlighted retrieving red planet samples as a key priority, which led to Mars Sample Return becoming intertwined with the Perseverance rover’s mission. The two projects were developed hand in hand. The original concept for Mars Sample Return, shared in 2020 , included a succession of multiple missions launching from Earth to Mars: a lander containing a Mars fetch rover to collect the samples and an ascent vehicle to return the samples to Earth by 2031 at the earliest. The ascent vehicle was intended to shoot out a football-size container holding the samples that would be captured by a separately launched ESA spacecraft orbiting Mars. Then, the ESA orbiter would head back to Earth, transferring the sample container into yet another vehicle that could deploy from the orbiter and safely land the samples on our planet. By 2022, the plan shifted : Perseverance would deliver the sample suite to the Mars Ascent Vehicle that would launch on a return journey. The lander would carry two small recovery helicopters, which could grab samples from the rover if Perseverance wasn’t in good enough condition to make the drive to a landing site. This nudged the return date to 2033. As things progressed, assessments from independent review boards pointed out how unwieldy and complex the retrieval process had become. The program’s budget ballooned to an eye-popping maximum of $11 billion and the estimated return date for the samples pushed to 2040. NASA also faced budget cuts for the 2024 and 2025 fiscal years, and the excessive costs of the mission led to waning political support for the program. The agency put out a call for cheaper, quicker and less complex proposals and, in January 2025, identified two strategies that relied on commercial partnerships or leaned on previously used Mars landing technology so as to not reinvent the wheel. That assessment came out just weeks before President Donald Trump took office and began the search for a new NASA administrator. The next sample return update, revealed with NASA’s fiscal year 2026 budget request , was an abrupt blow: “NASA plans to terminate the Mars Sample Return Program given that current architecture options remain unaffordable. It is anticipated that future missions to Mars will return samples for study on Earth.” The agency’s 2027 budget request didn’t mention the program at all. NASA spent about $2.5 billion on the Mars Sample Return through its cancellation, Dreier said. However, NASA administrator Jared Isaacman has mentioned that he’s interested in getting Perseverance’s samples delivered to Earth. “As I’ve said many times, I think retrieving the samples from Mars can lead to the most significant scientific breakthrough in human history,” Isaacman said at a news conference on August 30 after the successful launch of the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope . “There’s no question we’re going to go get samples, whether it’s robotic or whether it’s astronauts picking it up will be the question, and certainly the time frame associated with it.” Speaking at the All-In Summit in September, Isaacman blamed his predecessors for the program’s failures, noting “the prior administration canceled the Mars Sample Return mission that was on track to cost more than an aircraft carrier.” While the finger-pointing about the fate of the original program appears to continue, no additional details about next steps have emerged. China’s plan to fetch Mars samples is also complex, though arguably less so than NASA’s original design. Called Tianwen-3, the approach China is using draws on the success of Chang’e-6, a 2024 mission that retrieved the first samples from the moon’s far side. Tianwen-3 will include two launches: one for a lander, ascent vehicle and helicopter, and another for an orbiter and return vehicle to shuttle the samples to Earth, according to a study published by the mission team in 2025. The lander is equipped with a drill that can reach 2 meters (6.5 feet) beneath the Martian surface, the ideal place to search for signs of past or present life. The helicopter can also gather rock samples. Mission scientists plan for the lander to operate on Mars’ surface for about 70 days during sample collection, according to Yiliang Li, a core member of Tianwen-3’s science team who is aiding in the selection of landing sites. The Tianwen-3 team is narrowing down a list of 86 potential landing sites to identify regions where liquid water once existed on Mars, mineral-enriched regions and areas where ancient microbial activity could still be preserved, according to a 2024 study . Jezero Crater does not appear to be on the list. Ideally, the mission will retrieve two types of samples from ancient lake beds, said Li, a coauthor on both studies. The team is aiming to find one sample with iron oxides, which might have preserved cell shapes for billions of years, and a second sample that contains thick aquatic clays because they could contain ancient organic molecules created by living organisms, said Li, who is also a professor of astrobiology in the department of Earth and planetary sciences at the University of Hong Kong. Zengqian Hou, Tianwen-3’s chief scientist and economic geologist of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, announced in September at the International Deep Space Exploration Conference that engineers are currently building a prototype of Tianwen-3 . China also plans to build a planetary protection laboratory to house the samples, Hou said during the announcement. In recent years, NASA has focused increasingly on America-first messaging to position the US as leading the charge on marking milestones in space, including of beating China at being the first to land humans on Mars. A sample return win for China would certainly undermine that message. “American exceptionalism is being challenged in the high ground of space,” NASA Administrator Isaacman said while testifying on the 2027 NASA budget proposal in April. “To win, we cannot establish programs designed to be ‘too big to fail,’ but at the same time ‘too costly to succeed.’ Nor should it be throwing more money at the problem, but rather fixing the problems, concentrating resources on the mission and delivering outcomes.” Even as it ramps up the “space race” rhetoric in its efforts to return humans to the moon, the agency has made no mention of the fact that China may be the first to retrieve Martian samples — despite NASA already having a leg up with collected samples that just need to hitch a ride to Earth. “It’s remarkable that the US has advocated its leadership in this area of space exploration and just handed China the win in that one sector of the space race,” Rice said. Scientists remain hopeful that the Perseverance samples will be returned in some way, Horgan said. The ongoing work of industry partners is part of what’s keeping researchers optimistic. Lockheed Martin, for example, has worked with NASA on Mars missions and other sample return efforts in the past, which enabled the company to develop a streamlined concept to pick up the abandoned Perseverance samples, said Whitley Poyser, director of Lockheed Martin’s exploration mission area. The proposal included a fixed-price mission under $3 billion to return 30 of the rover’s samples to Earth no later than 2037. The concept revolved around using a lightweight Mars Ascent Vehicle, a small lander inspired by Lockheed Martin’s involvement in the InSight mission to Mars , and a compact Earth delivery system derived from lessons the company learned by assisting with the OSIRIS-Rex asteroid sample return mission , Poyser said. The company remains committed to their plan for retrieving samples from Mars and is prepared if the opportunity comes their way, she said. “The big area from a technical perspective that needs to mature is Mars ascent, especially if we are going to send someone there and send them back,” Poyser said. “We want to know how it’s going to work. All of those technologies are critical and they can be demonstrated through Mars Sample Return.” Even if the samples don’t contain signs of life, scientists say that knowledge could present intriguing possibilities, including the idea the spots may have been the work of prebiotic chemistry — the soup of elements, metals and organic carbon that could have formed a cell or living entity but didn’t reach its full potential. And if it turns out that life never existed on Mars, one of our planet’s closest neighbors, then why did it arise on Earth and not a world with similar conditions during the same time frame? Martian samples could tell the tale in a way that Earth’s rocks, shaped and lost over time due to erosion and other processes, can’t — and it’s up to the scientific community to share that message, Rice said. “I think there’s going to be a lot of advocacy for years to come, making sure that the general public is aware of how close we are to answering those big questions,” she said. “The rocks are there, they’re in their tubes, they’re ready. All we got to do is go get them.”

title: Nikon revokes first prize in Small World in Motion video competition over AI use
content: The winner of a prestigious scientific photography competition has been disqualified after organizers concluded that his use of generative AI broke the rules. Ning Xu was named the winner of the annual Nikon Small World in Motion competition in September, but his video received a number of critical comments from experts who questioned its use of AI. Nikon launched an investigation, and announced its conclusion in a statement Friday. “After thoroughly re-evaluating the video and supporting materials and consulting with members of our judging panel, Nikon has determined that the winning video did not comply with the competition rules regarding generative AI,” the statement reads, adding that the competition rankings have been adjusted. “This decision is based solely on the submitted video’s eligibility under the rules outlined for this competition. It should not be interpreted as a judgment of the entrant’s professional reputation, scientific contributions, or intent,” it said. Nikon also said it would revisit its rules and evaluation procedures for the annual competition in future. The new winner is a video showing a tiny roundworm and a single-celled Dileptus, a kind of single-celled microorganism, by Vietnamese researcher Nguyen Nam Nhat. Xu’s video captures the abnormal beating of airway cilia — hairlike structures that protrude from cells within the human body — in a child living with primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD), a rare genetic disorder. When Nikon posted the video on LinkedIn, it attracted criticism from scientists such as Edward Phelps, an associate professor at the University of Florida, who said there were “many serious problems with this video.” Phelps said that some of the biological structures shown in the footage do not behave as expected. “The microscopy community deserves an explanation from Nikon,” Phelps added. In response, in a series of comments on LinkedIn, Xu acknowledged that he had used AI. “AI was not used to generate the experimental movie, the cilia, or their motion,” he wrote. “It was applied afterwards to the reconstructed grayscale data to distinguish and color structures with similar morphology,” he added. CNN has reached out to Xu, who now works at the National University of Singapore as a research fellow, for further comment.

title: Paramedics experiment with AI note-taking tool
content:
Paramedics are experimenting with the use of AI assistants in frontline services.
North East Ambulance Service (NEAS) said it was in the middle of an eight-week trial studying the effectiveness of technology that records, transcribes and summarises patient conversations.
It said 38 individuals, ranging from paramedics to operational staff, were involved in the study and that it hoped the software may reduce staff workload.
The organisation's digital clinical lead Georgina Campbell said the trial would help the team better understand how emerging technology could be used "safely and effectively".
The AI tool works via the in-built iPad microphones used by ambulance staff, according to the NEAS, and is being used in real-world interactions between patients and paramedics.
All notes generated by the AI ambient voice technology, are reviewed and edited by a clinician before they are added to a patient's record, an NEAS spokesperson said.
The ambulance service said it had several hopes for the technology including the potential for it to improve record-keeping consistency and accuracy.
Campbell said: "This trial will help us understand how emerging technology can be used safely and effectively, while maintaining the high standards of care and record keeping that our patients and communities expect."
A spokesperson said the organisation would decide on the tool's future after the trial had concluded in November.

title: The island where locals say data centres are taking their water
content:
"Water! Water!" the crowd shouted as it stormed a compound with data centres, armed with empty plastic bottles and jerry cans.
There were about 300 of them, all residents on the Indonesian island of Batam, and they were furious that the taps at home had run dry, while the data centres in the new Nongsa Digital Park seemed to have enough water to protect their machines from overheating.
"Not a single drop has come through our taps for the last three months... Our water supply had been reliable until the data centres came," Dewi Susanti, one of the protesters, told the BBC.
People in her village, Bakau Serip, were now depending on tanker trucks that  dispensed "dirty, cloudy and smelly" water, she said.
Batam's water utility told the BBC it was working to improve supply, but did not comment on whether the disruption was linked to demand from the data centres.
But BP Batam, the agency overseeing trade and industry, blamed it on a prolonged dry spell and denied allegations from locals that water meant for homes was being channelled to data centres.
This is not the first such protest in Batam, whose shrinking reservoirs find themselves under more pressure as the island tries to transform itself into a digital hub.
Following protests in August and September, authorities told the firms opening data centres in Batam that they must build their own desalination plants instead of relying on reservoirs for freshwater.
But locals say they are increasingly concerned that they must now compete with servers for water.
"Reliable data on data centre water use in Indonesia remains scarce, partly because companies treat it as proprietary information," says Agus Hasan, a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology.
"We should build [data centres] rationally, transparently, and responsibly, and insist on seeing the numbers... [Otherwise] those kept in the dark while their taps run dry will push back, and rightly so," he adds.
A backlash has been building against data centres across the world, from the US to the UK to parts of Asia, as tech companies pour billions into AI infrastructure.
People are worried about how the huge, windowless buildings might change their neighbourhoods, the constant hum of machines, the security lights that could stay on all night, and the pressure this puts on water and energy resources.
While electricity powers the centres, the water keeps the servers from frying - engineers deploy elaborate cooling systems, which consume a lot of water.
Research in the US suggests a typical data centre consumes around 300,000 gallons of water a day, or about as much as 1,000 US households. A larger, 50MW facility could take as much water as 2,200 households per day, and enough electricity to power 22,000 homes, according to Malaysia's central bank.
It's unclear how much water or electricity the data centres in Batam are consuming.
But the island routinely faces water shortages, and the levels are worse this year, possibly because of a historic "super" El Niño.
Devoid of natural freshwater sources, Batam's 1.3 million people rely on rainwater collected in six artificial reservoirs.
Nongsa reservoir, which supplies water to Bakau Serip, where Dewi lives, would dry up over the next month with no rainfall, simulations by local environmental non-profit group Akar Bhumi Indonesia suggest.
"The water shortage is affecting our livelihoods... Money that should be used to buy rice is now spent on water drums," Dewi says. "My husband has to wait up overnight to get water, and then go straight to work the next morning."

title: Social media star from Jersey joins Blue Peter
content:
A social media star from Jersey has been unveiled as the newest presenter of Blue Peter.
Leo Olsson is best known for documenting "bucket list" personal challenges online, where he has almost 500,000 followers.
His first Blue Peter episode is due to be broadcast on November 20.
Olsson said: "It's a privilege to join a programme with such an incredible legacy".
Growing up in Jersey, Olsson started making videos when he was 12 years old.
As a teenager, he became well-known locally after writing letters to world leaders , seeking their best words of wisdom.
His desire to become a filmmaker lead him to a career as a content-creator, amassing more than 13 million likes and more than 454,000 followers across social media platforms.
Videos followed him as he took on challenges such as learning to play the piano, riding a unicycle and building a surfboard from scratch.
Speaking about joining the programme, he said : "There's no other show in the world like Blue Peter. It's all about adventure and not being afraid to try new things."
"Where else would you find a presenter trying to cross the Irish Sea in a Zorb ball, or walk a tightrope between the chimneys of Battersea Power Station?
"Growing up, all of my role models were the people I watched online and on television, so now I want show kids that you can go out and do whatever you want to do, take on a challenge, big or small."
In his first Blue Peter appearance, due to be broadcast on CBBC on Friday 20 November, Leo will earn his Blue Peter badge by joining a formation skydive being awarded his badge 4,000ft in the air.
Programme bosses described him as having "a sense of adventure and positivity" that made him the "perfect fit for Blue Peter".

title: AI minister warns 'likely' UK's cyber defences will be breached
content:
The UK's AI minister has warned it is "likely, if not inevitable" the country's cyber defences will at some point be breached.
Speaking at a press conference, Kanishka Narayan pointed to an incident of a rogue OpenAI agent hacking an Australian government website in June.
He said while no medical records are known to have been accessed in the attack, the incident should still "concern us".
Narayan said the government plans to put advanced AI to work to combat the threat, as he set out how the government plans to prepare for any serious future incidents.
The minister said the move would build on two existing pilots which have helped identify and fix over 1,000 vulnerabilities across government systems.
He said his message to the largest companies behind the world's most powerful AI systems was: "Listen when your scientists warn of serious dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviour. And if you cannot adequately control the risks, do not release the system."
In his speech, Narayan also confirmed scientists at the UK's AI watchdog, the AI Security Institute (AISI), were conducting "rigorous evaluations" of the latest generation of advanced AI models to "identify risks early" and "to test robust safeguards to help keep people safe".
AISI began evaluating risks of the latest frontier AI models, prior to their public release, shortly after it was established in November 2023.
But it was reported in September that the White House had asked some leading US labs not to share their models with the research organisation until its own tests were completed.
The move was viewed at the time as a blow to AISI - which has been championed by the UK government and its partners for advancing open, constructive and collaborative AI testing.
Microsoft president Brad Smith recently told the BBC the institute had helped cement the UK as the country best-placed to drive forward global regulation.
On Monday, Narayan said that in the last few weeks, the government had worked with the US "to retain access for Britain's AISI to the most powerful AI models before they are released".
He also said the UK would also look into creating stronger protections through the Cyber Security and Resilience bill, particularly at how serious AI incidents can be identified and reported.
Nuala Polo, UK Public Policy Lead at the Ada Lovelace Institute, said the announcement committed the government to "very little".
"Stronger protections will be 'considered', strengthening the Cyber Bill 'explored' and near-miss reporting 'looked at', with the detail to come later," she said.
"There is no new regulatory power, no timetable and no obligation on AI developers."
The announcement follows a series of incidents involving AI agents across major firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic acting outside human control and hacking into external systems.
On 9 September, Evan Hubinger, a top safety researcher at Anthropic, warned in a post on X that AI is advancing so quickly he believed there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.
The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown .
However, there are currently no global safety rules in place to regulate the companies and their technology. President Trump has called for the sector to regulate itself so that US firms do not lose out to Chinese rivals.

title: Make sure use of AI is safe, data watchdog warns
content:
Guernsey's data protection authority has warned the responsibility for protecting client data "can't be outsourced" amid concerns over the speed of artificial intelligence development.
Demands for laws and rules to control AI have grown after experts in the sector called for a slow down and last month it was revealed a "rogue" OpenAI agent hacked Australia's online medical system .
Brent Homan, commissioner for the Office of the Data Protection Authority, said Guernsey businesses needed to reflect on their use of AI seriously.
"Ultimately any organisation can outsource certain responsibilities, but they can't outsource their accountability," he said.
Homan said while the bailiwick was yet to see a reported AI-directed breach, it was important Guernsey companies were careful about security.
"It's really important for organisations to ensure that they have good contracts in place and assure themselves of the security of the third parties that they use," he said.
Matt Palmer, the director Guernsey and Jersey's cyber security centres, said AI was here to stay "whether we like it or not".
He said his organisation was adapting to the potential cybersecurity risks presented by AI but he felt positive about the bailiwick's position.
Companies should make use of existing resources to ensure their use of AI was safe, he added.
Palmer said: "I don't think it's quite the sort of goblin of fear that sometimes it is made out to be.
"What we need is careful testing, good controls, sensible and pragmatic adoption, we can deal with a lot of these risks. It is never going to be risk-free."

North East Ambulance Service is studying the effectiveness of AI in real-world patient interactions.
Hundreds of stores were targeted by the overnight hack, which spoiled fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.
Kanishka Narayan said the government will use advanced AI to strengthen the UK against cyber attacks.
Brad Smith calls for global rules on AI, and says the UK is in the "best position" to lead the charge.
Five police forces decide not to continue using software from a US tech firm after a two-year trial.
